main_text.p: sanguinis in corde) qui semper è cibo accedit, ultimam cordis tunicam elevan-tis, pulsum facit atque hoc semper sine ullâ intermissione facit. Unde in fine ejusdem capitis naturalem pulsum de-finiens, inquit, Φύξις ἡ δ᾽ ψυχῆς θερμαιν-νομένῃ πνεύματος. Pulsus est humoris concalescentis inflatio. Sed pudet sanè de antiquitate certare super re hoc nostro seculo accuratiùs repertâ. quâ vi Cor suâ diastole aperiat arterias at-que distendat fibrarum ope, aut in quo consistat illa facultas arteriarum, quâ dilatato corde arteriæ ad extremi-tates digitorum usque distendantur: quomodo teretes & cavæ arteriæ fi-bris suis parietes suos diducant non fa-cilius dixerit aut animo conceperit, quàm quomodo ter tria fiant decem. Cùm contrà facilè intelligatur san-guinem ex corde prorumpentem in arterias sanguine plenas, totum san-guinem, qui iis continetur; propter continuitatem, & rerum cunctarum

page.notes: The Greek words are printed partly in a cursive or damaged state; the reading of the Greek phrase is uncertain. The catchword "pleni-" is at the foot right. The final line is the hyphenated continuation. Some words near the binding edge are faint. Long s has been normalised to s.
